content: Corneal abrasions are a frequent reason for patients to seek medical attention for eye-related complaints. Despite the lack of robust evidence supporting their efficacy, eye patches are often recommended as a treatment for corneal abrasions. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of eye patching on the healing process and pain relief in individuals with corneal abrasions. The review aimed to assess whether patching the eye improves healing outcomes or alleviates pain. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, was performed. The search included studies published up to May 9, 2016, without restrictions on language or publication date. Randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing eye patching to no patching for simple corneal abrasions were included. Data collection involved independent risk of bias assessments and extraction of relevant data by two authors. The primary outcome was the rate of healing at 24, 48, and 72 hours, while secondary outcomes included pain levels, quality of life, adverse effects, and other related measures. The certainty of evidence was graded using the GRADE approach. A total of 12 trials involving 1,080 participants were included in the review. These trials were conducted in various countries, including the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Brazil, and Switzerland. Seven trials were found to have a high risk of bias in at least one domain, while one trial was judged to have a low risk of bias across all domains. The remaining trials had a mix of low and unclear risks of bias. The findings suggested that individuals who received an eye patch were slightly less likely to have a healed corneal abrasion after 24 hours compared to those who did not receive a patch (risk ratio [RR] 0.89, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.79 to 1.00, based on 7 trials with 531 participants; low-certainty evidence). By 48 hours, the healing rates were similar between the patch and no-patch groups (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.02, based on 6 trials with 497 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). At 72 hours, healing rates remained comparable (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.05, based on 4 trials with 430 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Participants in the patch group took slightly longer to heal, but the difference was minimal and likely clinically insignificant (mean difference [MD] 0.14 days longer, 95% CI 0 to 0.27 days longer, based on 6 trials with 642 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Pain levels were assessed in 10 trials, most of which used a visual analogue scale (VAS). However, the data could not be pooled due to skewed distributions. Overall, pain ratings were similar between the patch and no-patch groups. Two trials specifically reported the presence or absence of pain at 24 hours, but the results were inconclusive. There was a higher risk of reported pain in the patch group, but the confidence intervals were wide and included the possibility of both higher and lower risks of pain (RR 1.51, 95% CI 0.86 to 2.65, based on 2 trials with 193 participants; low-certainty evidence). Five trials compared the use of analgesics between the patch and no-patch groups. Data from three of these trials were combined, suggesting similar analgesic use in both groups, though with some uncertainty (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.32, based on 256 participants; low-certainty evidence). Commonly reported symptoms included photophobia, excessive tearing, foreign body sensation, and blurred vision, but there was little evidence to suggest significant differences in these symptoms between the patch and no-patch groups. One study assessed the impact of patching on activities of daily living (ADL) in children. While most ADL measures were unaffected, walking was reported to be more difficult with a patch (VAS 1.7 cm, standard deviation [SD] 2.1, versus 0.3 cm, SD 0.7). Complication rates were low across studies, and there was uncertainty regarding the relative effects of patching versus no patching on complications (RR 3.24, 95% CI 0.87 to 12.05, based on 8 trials with 660 participants; low-certainty evidence). Three trials reported compliance rates with treatment, finding that 22% of participants did not wear their eye patches during follow-up. Participants in the no-patch groups were more likely to receive additional treatments, such as antibiotics or cycloplegics, compared to those in the patch groups. Limited data were available on the effects of patching for larger abrasions exceeding 10 mm² in size. In conclusion, the evidence from these trials suggests that using an eye patch to treat simple corneal abrasions does not significantly improve healing rates or reduce pain. It is important to note that participants in the no-patch groups were more likely to receive additional treatments, such as antibiotics, which may have influenced the outcomes. The overall certainty of the evidence was judged to be moderate to low. Further research is needed to design and conduct higher-quality trials, particularly to evaluate the effectiveness of patching for larger corneal abrasions.
